n41714.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:regular-prime}
  \lean{IsRegularPrime}\leanok
An odd prime $p$ is \emph{regular} when $p$ does not divide the class
number of the $p$th cyclotomic field:
\[
  p \nmid h\bigl(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)\bigr).
\]
Otherwise $p$ is \emph{irregular}.  (In the formalisation the condition is
phrased as coprimality of $p$ with the cardinality of the class group of
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$, which is equivalent because $p$ is prime.)
\end{definition}

n41715.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:cm-real-subfield}
  \lean{NumberField.maximalRealSubfield}\leanok
For a number field $K$, let $K^+$ denote its maximal real subfield, the
largest subfield of $K$ all of whose complex embeddings are real.  When $K$
is a CM field, $K^+$ is the fixed field of complex conjugation, and
$[K : K^+] = 2$.  For $K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ this is the usual maximal real
subfield $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p + \zeta_p^{-1})$.
\end{definition}

n41716.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:class-number-h}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.h}\leanok
For a number field $K$, the class number $h(K)$ is the cardinality of the
ideal class group of its ring of integers:
\[
  h(K)=\#\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal O_K).
\]
\end{definition}

n41719.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
For a faithfully flat ring map $A \to B$, every ideal $J \subseteq A$
satisfies $JB \cap A = J$: the inclusion $J \subseteq JB \cap A$ is clear,
and the quotient map $A/J \to B/JB$ is injective by faithful flatness of
$B/JB$ over $A/J$.  It remains to note that $\mathcal O_L$ is faithfully
flat over $\mathcal O_{L^+}$: it is a finitely generated torsion-free
module over the Dedekind domain $\mathcal O_{L^+}$, hence projective, hence
flat, and $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_L \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathcal
O_{L^+}$ is surjective because the integral extension $\mathcal O_{L^+}
\subseteq \mathcal O_L$ satisfies lying-over.
\end{proof}

n41721.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Contract the equality $I\mathcal O_K=(b_0)$ back to $\mathcal O_{K^+}$.
The left-hand side contracts to $I$ by
\cref{thm:map-comap-ring-of-integers}.  For the right-hand side, the
contraction of $b_0\mathcal O_K$ contains $b_0\mathcal O_{K^+}$, and
conversely any element of $b_0 \mathcal O_K \cap \mathcal O_{K^+}$ is of
the form $b_0 c$ with $c \in K \cap \mathcal O_K = \mathcal O_{K^+}$
(using $b_0 \ne 0$; if $b_0 = 0$ then $I = 0$ is principal anyway).  Hence
$I=(b_0)$.
\end{proof}

n41723.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The extension $I\mathcal O_K$ is generated by elements coming from $K^+$,
and those elements are fixed by conjugation.  Conjugation is a ring
automorphism of $\mathcal O_K$, so it maps $I\mathcal O_K$ onto the ideal
generated by the conjugates of the generators, which is $I\mathcal O_K$
itself.
\end{proof}

n41725.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Two generators of the same nonzero principal ideal in a domain differ by a
unit: from $(a) = (\overline a)$ we get $\overline a = ua$ and $a = v
\overline a$ for some $u, v \in \mathcal O_K$, whence $a = vua$ and, since
$a \ne 0$, $vu = 1$.
\end{proof}

n41727.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Apply complex conjugation to $\overline a=ua$: since conjugation is an
involution, $a = \overline u\,\overline a = \overline u u a$.  As $a\ne0$,
cancellation in the domain $\mathcal O_K$ gives $u\overline u=1$.
\end{proof}

n41729.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
At every complex embedding $\sigma$ of $K$, conjugation corresponds to
complex conjugation of the image, so $|\sigma(u)|^2 = \sigma(u
\overline u) = 1$.  An algebraic integer all of whose conjugates have
absolute value $1$ is a root of unity (Kronecker's theorem), so $u$ is a
torsion unit.  The torsion subgroup of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)^\times$ for $p$ odd is
generated by $-1$ and $\zeta_p$, which gives the displayed form.
\end{proof}

n41730.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:conj-fixed-associate}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.exists_conj_fixed_associate_of_classification}\leanok
  \uses{thm:antisymmetric-unit-classification}
In the situation of \cref{thm:conj-generator-associated}, the generator $a$
may be replaced by an associate $b$ such that
\[
  \overline b=b
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  (b)=(a).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41731.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:antisymmetric-unit-classification}, the unit $u =
\overline a / a$ has the form $(-1)^n \zeta_p^m$.  Since $p$ is odd, every
power of $\zeta_p$ is a square in $\langle\zeta_p\rangle$, and the sign can
be absorbed: write $u = w/\overline w$ for a suitable root of unity $w$
(concretely, a power of $\zeta_p$ chosen so that $w^2$ accounts for
$\zeta_p^m$, possibly times $-1$).  Then $b := w a$ satisfies
$\overline b = \overline w\,\overline a = \overline w u a = w a = b$,
and $b$ is an associate of $a$, so it generates the same ideal.
\end{proof}

n41733.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
For a CM field, $K^+$ is exactly the fixed field of conjugation, so the
element $b$ lies in $K^+$.  Being integral over $\mathbb{Z}$, it lies in
$K^+ \cap \mathcal O_K = \mathcal O_{K^+}$.
\end{proof}

n41735.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Let $I$ be such an ideal; we may assume $I \ne 0$.  Choose a generator $a$
of $I\mathcal O_K$.  The extended ideal is conjugation-stable
(\cref{thm:ideal-map-conj}), so \cref{thm:conj-generator-associated}
produces a unit $u$ with $\overline a = ua$, and
\cref{thm:conj-unit-mul-one} shows $u\overline u = 1$.  The classification
of such units (\cref{thm:antisymmetric-unit-classification}) lets us
replace $a$ by a conjugation-fixed associate $b$ with $(b) = I\mathcal O_K$
(\cref{thm:conj-fixed-associate}).  By
\cref{thm:mem-ring-of-integers-conj-self}, $b$ descends to an element $b_0
\in \mathcal O_{K^+}$, and \cref{thm:is-principal-map-span-singleton}
contracts the equality $I\mathcal O_K = (b_0)$ to $I = (b_0)$.
\end{proof}

n41738.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
A group homomorphism is injective when its kernel is trivial.  If an ideal
class of $\mathcal O_{K^+}$ maps to the trivial class, a representative
ideal becomes principal after extension to $\mathcal O_K$; by
\cref{thm:is-principal-after-extension} the representative was already
principal, so the class is trivial.
\end{proof}

n41740.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:class-group-map-injective}, $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal O_{K^+})$ embeds as
a subgroup of the finite group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$, and Lagrange's theorem
gives the divisibility of cardinalities.
\end{proof}

n41743.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Multiply the defining quotient of \cref{def:class-number-hminus} by
$h^+(K)$; this is legitimate in $\mathbb{N}$ because $h^+(K) \mid h(K)$
(\cref{thm:hplus-divides-h}) and $h^+(K) \ne 0$.
\end{proof}

n41744.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:dvd-h-iff-dvd-hminus-from-plus-to-minus}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.dvd_h_iff_dvd_hMinus_of_dvd_hPlus_imp}\leanok
  \uses{thm:h-factorisation}
Assume that a separate argument proves the implication
\[
  p\mid h^+(K)\Longrightarrow p\mid h^-(K).
\]
Then
\[
  p\mid h(K)\Longleftrightarrow p\mid h^-(K).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41745.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Write $h(K) = h^+(K)\,h^-(K)$ by \cref{thm:h-factorisation}.  If $p \mid
h(K)$, then by primality $p\mid h^+(K)$ or $p\mid h^-(K)$, and the first
alternative implies the second by hypothesis; either way $p \mid h^-(K)$.
Conversely $h^-(K)$ divides $h(K)$, so $p \mid h^-(K)$ implies
$p \mid h(K)$.
\end{proof}

n41746.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:dirichlet-character}
  \lean{DirichletCharacter}\leanok
A \emph{Dirichlet character} modulo $N$ with values in a commutative ring
$R$ is a multiplicative character of $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ with values in
$R^\times$, extended by zero to all of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.  A character $\chi$
modulo $N > 1$ is \emph{even} if $\chi(-1) = 1$ and \emph{odd} if
$\chi(-1) = -1$.  In this chapter the modulus is the odd prime $p$, in
which case every nontrivial character is primitive and exactly
$(p-1)/2$ of the characters are odd.
\end{definition}

n41747.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:generalized-bernoulli}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.BernoulliGen}\leanok
  \uses{def:dirichlet-character}
For a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $N$ and $n \ge 0$, the
\emph{generalised Bernoulli number} is
\[
  B_{n,\chi}
  \;=\;
  N^{\,n-1} \sum_{a \bmod N} \chi(a)\, B_n\!\left(\frac{a}{N}\right),
\]
where $B_n(X)$ is the $n$th Bernoulli polynomial.  For nontrivial $\chi$
the case $n = 1$ simplifies to
\[
  B_{1,\chi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{a=1}^{N} \chi(a)\,a ,
\]
because $\sum_a \chi(a) = 0$ kills the constant term of
$B_1(X) = X - \tfrac12$.  The class-number formula only uses the values
$B_{1,\chi^{-1}}$ for odd $\chi$.
\end{definition}

n41748.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:teichmuller}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.teichmullerCharQp}\leanok
  \uses{def:dirichlet-character}
The \emph{Teichm\"uller character} of the prime $p$ is the unique character
\[
  \omega\colon\left(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\right)^\times\to\mathbb{Z}_p^\times
\]
such that $\omega(a) \equiv a \pmod p$ and $\omega(a)^{p-1} = 1$ for every
$a$; its values are the $(p-1)$st roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_p$.  Composing with
the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}_p \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}_p$ gives the $\mathbb{Q}_p$-valued Dirichlet
character used below.  The characters $\omega^j$ for $0 \le j \le p-2$
exhaust the characters modulo $p$, and $\omega^j$ is odd exactly when $j$
is odd.
\end{definition}

n41750.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By the von Staudt--Clausen theorem, the denominator of $B_n$ (for $n$ even,
the only nontrivial case) is the product of the primes $q$ with
$(q-1)\mid n$.  If $p$ occurred, then $p - 1 \le n$, contradicting
$n < p-1$.  Hence the denominator is prime to $p$ and $B_n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$.
\end{proof}

n41752.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
This is the rational form of \cref{thm:bernoulli-padicInt-below}: a
rational number lies in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ exactly when its reduced denominator is
prime to $p$.
\end{proof}

n41754.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The denominator of $B_n$ is prime to $p$ by
\cref{thm:bernoulli-den-coprime}, and $n < p-1 < p$ is also prime to $p$,
so $B_n/n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$.  In $\mathbb{Z}_p$ the non-units are exactly the elements of
$p\mathbb{Z}_p$; since the denominator and $n$ are $p$-adic units, $B_n/n \in
p\mathbb{Z}_p$ holds precisely when $p$ divides the numerator of $B_n$.
\end{proof}

n41756.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
This is the standard congruence linking generalised Bernoulli values of
Teichm\"uller powers to classical Bernoulli numbers.  Writing
$B_{1,\omega^j} = \tfrac1p \sum_a \omega^j(a)\,a$ and using
$\omega(a) \equiv a^{p^r}$ to high $p$-adic accuracy, the sum is compared
with the power sum $\sum_a a^{\,j+1}$, which Faulhaber's formula relates to
$B_{j+1}$; the hypothesis that $j+1$ is divisible by neither $p$ nor $p-1$
makes the comparison factor a $p$-adic unit and keeps the error terms in
$p\mathbb{Z}_p$.
\end{proof}

n41758.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The analytic class-number formula for the totally real field $K^+$
expresses $h^+$ through the residue of the Dedekind zeta function
$\zeta_{K^+}$.  Factoring $\zeta_{K^+}(s) = \zeta(s)\prod_{\chi \text{
even},\ \chi\ne1} L(s,\chi)$ over the even characters and inserting the
classical evaluation of $L(1,\chi)$ for even primitive $\chi$ --- the
displayed Gauss-sum-and-logarithm expression --- gives the formula.
\end{proof}

n41760.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The proof splits into the cases $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and $p\equiv3\pmod4$.  A
non-quadratic odd character $\chi$ is paired with its distinct inverse
$\chi^{-1}$ (also odd), and the identity
$\tau(\chi)\tau(\chi^{-1}) = \chi(-1)\,p = -p$ evaluates each pair.  When
$p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ the quadratic character is odd and unpaired; it
contributes the classical quadratic Gauss sum $i\sqrt p$.  Counting pairs
in the two cases and collecting signs and powers of $i$ gives the stated
value.
\end{proof}

n41762.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Purely formal: the assembly theorem consumes the Gauss product in a
normalised shape (with the analytic constants of the odd $L$-value formula
distributed over the product), and this normalisation is a finite algebraic
rewriting of \cref{thm:raw-gauss-product}.
\end{proof}

n41763.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:hminus-formula-from-inputs}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.hMinus_formula_of_residue_and_hPlus_cyclotomic_and_gauss}\leanok
  \uses{def:class-number-hminus, def:generalized-bernoulli,
  thm:hplus-even-lvalues, thm:cyclotomic-gauss-goal}
Assume the factorisation of the Dedekind zeta residue of $K$ into the even
and odd $L$-value products, the $h^+$ formula of
\cref{thm:hplus-even-lvalues}, and the packaged Gauss-product identity.
Then
\[
  h^-(K)
  =
  2p\prod_{\chi\ \mathrm{odd}}
    \left(-\frac12 B_{1,\chi^{-1}}\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41764.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Divide the analytic class-number formula of $K$ (in residue form) by that
of $K^+$.  Using $h = h^+ h^-$, the quotient expresses $h^-$ times the
ratio of the analytic constants as the product of the odd $L$-values
$L(1,\chi)$.  Substituting the odd $L$-value formula
\[
  L(1,\chi) = \frac{\pi i\,\tau(\chi)}{p}\,B_{1,\chi^{-1}}
\]
for each odd $\chi$ and cancelling the powers of $\pi$, $i$ and the Gauss
sums against the analytic constants --- this is exactly what the packaged
Gauss-product identity provides --- leaves the displayed product of
generalised Bernoulli factors with the prefactor $2p$.
\end{proof}

n41766.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Supply the three inputs of \cref{thm:hminus-formula-from-inputs}: the
residue of $\zeta_K$ factors over the nontrivial characters into the even
and odd $L$-value products; the even product is converted by
\cref{thm:hplus-even-lvalues}; and the Gauss hypothesis is
\cref{thm:cyclotomic-gauss-goal}.
\end{proof}

n41768.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Starting from \cref{thm:hminus-formula}, index the odd characters modulo
$p$ as $\omega^j$ with $j$ odd, $1 \le j \le p-2$.  The boundary exponent
$j = p-2$ plays a special role: the combination of the prefactor $2p$ with
the boundary factor $-\tfrac12 B_{1,\omega^{p-2}}$ is a $p$-adic integer
congruent to $1$ modulo $p$, so it can be absorbed into the error term
$pz$, leaving the product over odd $j < p-2$.
\end{proof}

n41770.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Replace each factor $B_{1,\omega^j}$ in \cref{thm:hminus-teichmuller-mod-p}
by the congruent classical quotient $B_{j+1}/(j+1)$ from
\cref{thm:teichmuller-bernoulli-congruence}; for odd $j < p-2$ the index
$j+1$ is even with $0 < j+1 < p-1$, so the hypotheses of the congruence
hold.  Each replacement changes the product by an element of $p\mathbb{Z}_p$ times
a product of $p$-adic integers --- integrality of the remaining factors is
\cref{lem:padic-bernoulli-factor} --- so all errors collect into a single
multiple of $p$.
\end{proof}

n41771.content:
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:odd-index-to-k}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.exists_odd_index_iff_exists_k}\leanok
For any predicate $Q$ on natural numbers,
\[
  \bigl(\exists j,\ j<p-2,\ j\ \mathrm{odd},\ Q(j+1)\bigr)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\exists k,\ 1\le k,\ 2k\le p-3,\ Q(2k)\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

n41772.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
If $j$ is odd, write $j=2k-1$ with $k \ge 1$, so $j+1=2k$, and $j < p-2$
becomes $2k \le p-3$ after parity bookkeeping.  Conversely, an even index
$2k$ in Kummer's range corresponds to the odd index $j=2k-1 < p-2$.
\end{proof}

n41773.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:hminus-bernoulli-final}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.p_dvd_hMinus_iff_p_dvd_some_bernoulli}\leanok
  \uses{thm:hminus-bernoulli-mod-p, lem:padic-bernoulli-factor,
  lem:odd-index-to-k}
For $p$ odd,
\[
  p\mid h^-(K)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \exists k,\ 1\le k,\ 2k\le p-3,\quad
  p\mid\operatorname{num}(B_{2k}).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41774.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:hminus-bernoulli-mod-p}, $h^-$ is congruent modulo $p$ to the
finite product of the $p$-adic integers $-\tfrac12 B_{j+1}/(j+1)$ over odd
$j < p-2$.  The factor $-\tfrac12$ and the denominator $j+1$ are $p$-adic
units in this range, so by \cref{lem:padic-bernoulli-factor} each factor is
a non-unit exactly when $p$ divides $\operatorname{num}(B_{j+1})$.  A
product of $p$-adic integers lies in $p\mathbb{Z}_p$ exactly when one of the
factors does, so $p \mid h^-$ holds precisely when some numerator in the
range is divisible by $p$.  Finally \cref{lem:odd-index-to-k} converts the
odd index $j$ into the classical range $1\le k$, $2k\le p-3$ with
$2k = j+1$.
\end{proof}

n41776.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Contrapositive of one direction of \cref{thm:hminus-bernoulli-final}: a
numerator divisible by $p$ in the range would force $p\mid h^-(K)$.
\end{proof}

n41777.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:real-cyclotomic-unit}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.realCyclotomicUnit}\leanok
For $2\le a\le (p-1)/2$, the \emph{real cyclotomic unit} $\varepsilon_a$ is
the unit of $\mathcal O_{K^+}$ obtained by descending the product of the
cyclotomic unit $(1-\zeta_p^a)/(1-\zeta_p)$ of $\mathcal O_K$ with its
complex conjugate:
\[
  \varepsilon_a
  \;=\;
  \frac{(1-\zeta_p^a)\,(1-\zeta_p^{-a})}{(1-\zeta_p)\,(1-\zeta_p^{-1})} .
\]
This element is fixed by complex conjugation, hence lies in
$(\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times$.
\end{definition}

n41780.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:normalizedCPlus}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.normalizedCPlus}\leanok
  \uses{def:CPlus}
For $2 \le a \le (p-1)/2$, the \emph{normalised cyclotomic unit} is
\[
  \xi_a \;=\; \zeta_p^{\,(1-a)/2}\,\frac{1-\zeta_p^a}{1-\zeta_p},
\]
where the exponent $(1-a)/2$ is read modulo $p$.  The twist by the root of
unity makes $\xi_a$ fixed by complex conjugation, so it defines a unit of
$\mathcal O_{K^+}$.  The normalised subgroup $C^+_{\mathrm{norm}}$ is
generated by $-1$ and the units $\xi_a$.
\end{definition}

n41784.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:normalized-square}, $C^+ \subseteq C^+_{\mathrm{norm}}$ and
every square of a normalised generator lies in $C^+$, so the quotient
$C^+_{\mathrm{norm}}/C^+$ is an elementary abelian $2$-group of bounded
rank; in particular the two indices differ by a power of $2$.  Since $p$
is odd, multiplying or dividing by a power of $2$ does not affect
$p$-divisibility.
\end{proof}

n41785.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:EPlus}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.EPlus}\leanok
The ambient group for the saturation argument is the full unit group
\[
  E^+ = (\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times .
\]
\end{definition}

n41790.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Induction over membership in the subgroup generated by $-1$ and the
$\varepsilon_a$: each generator trivially has such an expression, the
identity is the empty product, and the set of elements admitting an
expression is closed under multiplication (add the exponent vectors) and
inverses (negate them).
\end{proof}

n41792.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Let $x \in C^+$ be a $p$th power in $E^+$, and write $x = (-1)^s \prod_a
\varepsilon_a^{e_a}$ by \cref{thm:exists-CPlusExponentProduct}.  By
hypothesis $p \mid e_a$ for every $a$.  Since $p$ is odd, $(-1)^s =
\bigl((-1)^s\bigr)^p$, so
\[
  x = \Bigl((-1)^s\prod_a\varepsilon_a^{\,e_a/p}\Bigr)^{\!p}
\]
exhibits $x$ as the $p$th power of an element of $C^+$.
\end{proof}

n41794.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The group-theoretic statement is: a finite-index $p$-saturated subgroup $H
\le E$ whose inclusion captures the $p$-torsion of $E/H$ has index prime to
$p$.  Indeed, if $p$ divided the index, the finite abelian quotient $E/H$
would contain an element of order exactly $p$, say the class of $x$; then
$x^p \in H$ is a $p$th power in $E$, so by saturation $x^p = y^p$ with
$y\in H$, and $x/y$ is a $p$-torsion unit of $E$ not in $H$.  For
$E = E^+$, torsion units of the totally real field $K^+$ are $\pm1$, and
$-1 \in C^+$ by construction, so no such element exists --- a
contradiction.  Finiteness of the index is supplied by the cyclotomic-unit
index theory (the units $\varepsilon_a$ are a full-rank family).
\end{proof}

n41795.content:
\begin{definition}\label{def:kummerLogRank}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.CyclotomicUnits.kummerLogRank}\leanok
Set
\[
  r \;=\; \frac{p-3}{2},
\]
the common cardinality of the set of standard generators
$\varepsilon_2,\ldots,\varepsilon_{(p-1)/2}$ and of the even index set
$\{2j : 1 \le j,\ 2j \le p-3\}$ of Kummer's range.
\end{definition}

n41797.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:kummer-log-vandermonde}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.CyclotomicUnits.concreteKummerLogMatrix_eq_diagonal_mul_vandermonde}\leanok
  \uses{def:concreteKummerLogMatrix}
The Kummer logarithm matrix factors as
\[
  M = D \cdot V,
\]
where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of Bernoulli factors (the $j$th diagonal
entry being a unit multiple of the reduction of $B_{2j}/2j$) and $V$ is a
Vandermonde-type matrix built from Teichm\"uller values.
\end{theorem}

n41798.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Expand the completed logarithm of each generator in the Dwork basis and
compute the coefficients.  Each entry of $M$ splits as a product of a
factor depending only on the row $j$ --- the Bernoulli factor --- and a
factor of the form $\eta_a^{\,2j}$ depending on the column through a
Teichm\"uller node $\eta_a$.  Collecting the row factors into a diagonal
matrix exhibits the remaining matrix as a Vandermonde matrix in the nodes
$\eta_a^2$.
\end{proof}

n41800.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The nodes are the values $\eta_a^2$ for $2 \le a \le (p-1)/2$; they are
pairwise distinct and distinct from $1$, because the Teichm\"uller
character is injective on $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ and squaring is two-to-one with
the representatives $a$ chosen in a half-system.  A Vandermonde
determinant in distinct nodes is a product of nonzero differences, hence
nonzero.
\end{proof}

n41802.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:kummer-log-vandermonde}, $\det M = \det D \cdot \det V$, and
$\det V \ne 0$ by \cref{thm:vandermonde-nonzero}.  Hence $\det M \ne 0$
exactly when $\det D = \prod_j D_{jj} \ne 0$, i.e.\ when every diagonal
entry is nonzero.
\end{proof}

n41804.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The factor is the reduction modulo $p$ of a $p$-integral rational
expression which is a $p$-adic unit multiple of $B_{2j}/2j$; in the range
$2j \le p-3$, both $2j$ and the denominator of $B_{2j}$ are prime to $p$
(\cref{lem:padic-bernoulli-factor}).  So the reduction vanishes exactly
when $p$ divides the numerator of $B_{2j}$.
\end{proof}

n41805.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:kummer-log-det-bernoulli}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.CyclotomicUnits.kummerLogMatrix_det_ne_zero_iff_bernoulli_nonzero}\leanok
  \uses{thm:kummer-det-bernoulli-factor, thm:bernoulliFactor-num}
The Kummer logarithm determinant is nonzero precisely when no Bernoulli
numerator in Kummer's range is divisible by $p$:
\[
  \det M\ne0
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \forall j,\ 1\le j,\ 2j\le p-3,\quad
  p\nmid\operatorname{num}(B_{2j}).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41806.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
\Cref{thm:kummer-det-bernoulli-factor} reduces the determinant condition to
the nonvanishing of every diagonal Bernoulli factor, and
\cref{thm:bernoulliFactor-num} translates each of those conditions into
nondivisibility of the corresponding numerator.  The finite index set of
the matrix is identified with the classical range $1\le j$, $2j\le p-3$.
\end{proof}

n41808.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The completed logarithm is a homomorphism on the relevant units: it turns
the exponent product into the corresponding integer combination of the
logarithms of the generators, and it sends a $p$th power $y^p$ to
$p\log y$.  Equating the two expressions exhibits the combination
$\sum_a e_a \log \varepsilon_a$ as $p$ times an element of the fixed
subalgebra.  (The sign $(-1)^s$ is killed by the logarithm.)
\end{proof}

n41810.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Take coordinates in the Dwork basis.  The $j$th coordinate of the
combination $\sum_a e_a \log\varepsilon_a$ is the $j$th entry of the
matrix-vector product $Me$ (before reduction).  Divisibility by $p$ of the
combination makes every coordinate divisible by $p$, i.e.\ every entry of
$Me$ vanishes after reduction modulo $p$.
\end{proof}

n41812.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$, a square matrix with nonzero determinant is
invertible, so its kernel is trivial.
\end{proof}

n41814.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Apply \cref{thm:completed-log-relation} to the $p$th-power relation, then
\cref{thm:kummer-mulvec-zero} converts the logarithmic divisibility into
$Me=0$, and \cref{thm:kummer-linear-algebra} forces $e=0$ modulo $p$.
\end{proof}

n41816.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
\Cref{thm:kummer-log-exponents-zero} is exactly the exponent-vanishing
hypothesis of the saturation criterion
\cref{thm:CPlus-pSaturated-exponents}.
\end{proof}

n41819.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Both inclusions are checked on generators.  A normalised generator $\xi_a$
times a root of unity recovers the cyclotomic unit
$(1-\zeta_p^a)/(1-\zeta_p)$, whose product with its conjugate is
$\varepsilon_a = \xi_a^2$; conversely each $\varepsilon_a$ is the square of
$\xi_a$, so the two subgroups generate each other up to squares and signs.
\end{proof}

n41820.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:deleted-fourier-kummer-dirichlet}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.kummerDirichletDeterminant_of_deletedFourier}\leanok
The deleted-Fourier determinant identity supplies the Kummer--Dirichlet
determinant hypothesis required by the Sinnott index pipeline: the
regulator-type determinant of the cyclotomic-unit family is, up to an
explicit nonzero factor, a product of the character sums
$\sum_a \chi(a) \log|1-e^{2\pi i a/p}|$ over the even nontrivial
characters.
\end{theorem}

n41821.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The logarithmic embeddings of the cyclotomic units form a matrix whose
group-theoretic structure (rows and columns indexed by a cyclic group) is
diagonalised by the discrete Fourier transform with one character deleted.
Composing the resulting determinant identity with the regulator identity
for the cyclotomic-unit family produces exactly the Kummer--Dirichlet
determinant needed downstream.
\end{proof}

n41822.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:index-pprimary-aux}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.cyclotomicUnitIndex_primeConductor_pPrimary_aux}\leanok
  \uses{thm:index-subgroup-eq-CPlus, thm:deleted-fourier-kummer-dirichlet,
  thm:CPlus-normalized-index, def:class-number-hplus}
For $p\ge5$, the normalised cyclotomic-unit index has the same
$p$-divisibility as $h^+$:
\[
  p\mid[(\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times:C^+_{\mathrm{norm}}]
  \Longleftrightarrow
  p\mid h^+(K).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41823.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
This is Sinnott's prime-conductor index theorem: for prime conductor the
index of the circular units in the full unit group equals $h^+$.  The
deleted-Fourier determinant of
\cref{thm:deleted-fourier-kummer-dirichlet} provides the determinant
computation at the heart of the proof,
\cref{thm:index-subgroup-eq-CPlus} identifies the index subgroup with the
one used here, and \cref{thm:CPlus-normalized-index} transfers
$p$-divisibility between the standard and normalised indices.
\end{proof}

n41825.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
For $p=3$ the field $K^+$ is $\mathbb{Q}$: the normalised subgroup is the whole
unit group $\{\pm1\}$ and $h^+=1$, so both sides are false.  For $p\ge5$
this is \cref{thm:index-pprimary-aux}.
\end{proof}

n41826.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:bernoulli-nonzero-index}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.not_dvd_cyclotomicUnitIndex_of_bernoulli_nonzero}\leanok
  \uses{thm:kummer-log-det-bernoulli, thm:kummer-log-det-saturation,
  thm:not-dvd-index-of-pSaturated}
Let $p$ be an odd prime.  Suppose that
\[
  \forall j,\ 1\le j,\ 2j\le p-3,\quad
  p\nmid\operatorname{num}(B_{2j}).
\]
Then
\[
  p\nmid[(\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times:C^+].
\]
\end{theorem}

n41827.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
If $p=3$, Kummer's range is empty, $K^+ = \mathbb{Q}$, the group $C^+$ is the full
unit group $\{\pm1\}$, and the index is $1$.  For $p\ge5$,
\cref{thm:kummer-log-det-bernoulli} identifies the Bernoulli nonvanishing
hypothesis with the nonvanishing of the Kummer logarithm determinant.  By
\cref{thm:kummer-log-det-saturation}, the subgroup $C^+$ is then
$p$-saturated in the full unit group, and
\cref{thm:not-dvd-index-of-pSaturated} concludes that the index is prime
to $p$.
\end{proof}

n41829.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{thm:hminus-nondiv-to-bernoulli-nondiv}, the hypothesis
$p\nmid h^-(K)$ implies that no Bernoulli numerator in Kummer's range is
divisible by $p$, so \cref{thm:bernoulli-nonzero-index} gives
\[
  p\nmid[(\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times:C^+].
\]
Suppose for contradiction that $p\mid h^+(K)$.  The prime-conductor index
theorem (\cref{thm:sinnott-index-pprimary}) then gives $p \mid
[(\mathcal O_{K^+})^\times:C^+_{\mathrm{norm}}]$, and by
\cref{thm:CPlus-normalized-index} this is equivalent to $p$ dividing the
ordinary $C^+$ index --- a contradiction.
\end{proof}

n41831.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Contrapositive of \cref{thm:not-dvd-hplus-of-not-dvd-hminus-units}: if
$p\nmid h^-(K)$, that theorem gives $p\nmid h^+(K)$.
\end{proof}

n41832.content:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:dvd-h-iff-bernoulli-units}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.dvd_h_iff_exists_dvd_bernoulli_units}\leanok
  \uses{thm:dvd-h-iff-dvd-hminus-from-plus-to-minus,
  thm:hplus-to-hminus-units, thm:hminus-bernoulli-final}
For an odd prime $p$ and the $p$th cyclotomic field $K$,
\[
  p\mid h(K)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \exists k,\ 1\le k,\ 2k\le p-3,\quad
  p\mid\operatorname{num}(B_{2k}).
\]
\end{theorem}

n41833.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The implication $p\mid h^+(K)\Rightarrow p\mid h^-(K)$ is
\cref{thm:hplus-to-hminus-units}; feeding it to
\cref{thm:dvd-h-iff-dvd-hminus-from-plus-to-minus} converts $p\mid h(K)$
into $p\mid h^-(K)$.  The minus class-number criterion
(\cref{thm:hminus-bernoulli-final}) rewrites the latter as the existence of
a Bernoulli numerator in Kummer's range divisible by $p$.
\end{proof}

n41835.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By \cref{def:regular-prime}, $p$ is regular if and only if $p$ is coprime
to the class number of the $p$th cyclotomic field; since $p$ is prime,
this is equivalent to $p\nmid h(K)$.  By
\cref{thm:dvd-h-iff-bernoulli-units}, the negation of $p\mid h(K)$ is
exactly the assertion that no $k$ in the range $1\le k$, $2k\le p-3$
satisfies $p\mid\operatorname{num}(B_{2k})$, which is the displayed
universal nondivisibility.
\end{proof}

n41845.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Divisibility of the numerator by $p$ is equivalent to $q \in p\mathbb{Z}_p$, which is
invariant under perturbation by elements of $p\mathbb{Z}_p$.
\end{proof}

n41849.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By the von Staudt--Clausen theorem,
\[
  B_n + \sum_{(q-1)\mid n} \frac{1}{q} \in \mathbb{Z},
\]
the sum running over primes $q$ with $(q-1)\mid n$.  Since $(p-1)\mid n$, the
prime $p$ occurs in the correction sum, so $B_n + 1/p$ has denominator prime
to $p$.  If $p$ divided $\operatorname{num}(B_n)$, then adding $1/p$ would
produce a denominator divisible by $p$, a contradiction; by
\cref{lem:num-of-divided} the same holds for the divided numerator.
\end{proof}

n41851.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
By von Staudt--Clausen, $B_n$ differs from an integer by the correction
sum $\sum_{(q-1)\mid n} 1/q$.  Each summand has prime denominator, so
multiplying by $p$ clears the single possible factor of $p$ in the
denominator and leaves a $p$-adic integer.
\end{proof}

n41853.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Euler's formula gives
\[
  \zeta(2k) \;=\; (-1)^{k+1}\,\frac{B_{2k}\,(2\pi)^{2k}}{2\,(2k)!},
\]
and $\zeta(2k) \ge 1$, so $|B_{2k}| \ge 2\,(2k)!/(2\pi)^{2k}$.  Dividing by
$2k$ yields the claim.
\end{proof}

n41855.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The lower bound of \cref{thm:bernoulli-growth-bound} tends to infinity:
factorial growth beats the geometric factor $(2\pi^2)^{k}$ in the
denominator.
\end{proof}

n41857.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The indices $C \cdot 2^t$ are even and tend to infinity, so
\cref{thm:bernoulli-growth-tendsto} applies along this subsequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}\label{def:irregular-base}
  \lean{KummerCriterion.irregularBase}\leanok
For a finite set $S$ of natural numbers put $M(S) = \max(3, \max S)$ and
\[
  C(S) \;=\; 2 \cdot M(S)! \,.
\]
\end{definition}

n41860.content:

$q \le M(S)$, so $q - 1$ is a positive integer at most $M(S)$ and therefore
divides $M(S)!$.
\end{proof}

n41862.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
If $q = 2$ this is trivial.  Otherwise $q$ divides $M(S)!$, hence
$q \le M(S)$, and as before $(q-1) \mid M(S)! \mid m$.
\end{proof}

n41864.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
This is Voronoi's congruence (see e.g.\ \cite[Chapter~15]{ireland-rosen}).
Writing $ja = p\lfloor ja/p \rfloor + r_j$
with $r_j$ the residue of $ja$, summing $r_j^k$ over $j$ and expanding by the
binomial theorem identifies the two sides modulo $p$, using Faulhaber's
formula for power sums and the von Staudt--Clausen integrality
(\cref{lem:vonstaudt-p-integral}) to control the Bernoulli denominators of
the lower-order terms.
\end{proof}

n41866.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Choose a primitive root $a$ modulo $p$ and apply \cref{thm:voronoi-congruence}
to both indices.  Since $m \equiv n \pmod{p-1}$, Fermat's little theorem gives
$a^m \equiv a^n$ and $j^{m-1}\equiv j^{n-1} \pmod p$ for all $j$, so the two
Voronoi sums agree modulo $p$.  Subtracting the two instances yields
$(a^{n}-1)\bigl(B_m/m - B_n/n\bigr) \equiv 0 \pmod p$, and because $a$ is a
primitive root with $(p-1)\nmid n$ the factor $a^{n}-1$ is a $p$-adic unit,
giving the congruence.
\end{proof}

n41868.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
It remains to lift the restriction $p \ge 5$ of
\cref{thm:kummer-congruence-gefive} to all odd primes.  The only other odd
prime is $p = 3$, where $p - 1 = 2$ divides every even index; the hypothesis
$(p-1)\nmid n$ is then unsatisfiable, so there is nothing left to prove.
\end{proof}

n41870.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The residue is nonzero precisely because $(p-1)\nmid m$, and it inherits
parity from $m$ since $p-1$ is even.
\end{proof}

n41872.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
If $p$ is irregular, \cref{thm:bernoulli-witness-of-irregular} produces a
witness $B_{2k}$ in Kummer's range; since $2k \le p-3 < p$, the index is a
unit modulo $p$ and the divisibility passes to the divided numerator.

Conversely, suppose $p\mid\operatorname{num}(B_m/m)$ with $m$ positive and
even.  By \cref{thm:vonstaudt-not-dvd-divided}, necessarily $(p-1)\nmid m$.
Let $m'$ be the positive residue of \cref{lem:positive-residue}.  The full
Kummer congruence (\cref{thm:kummer-congruence-full}) gives
$B_m/m \equiv B_{m'}/m' \pmod p$, so $p\mid\operatorname{num}(B_{m'}/m')$ by
\cref{lem:num-transport}, hence $p \mid \operatorname{num}(B_{m'})$ by
\cref{lem:num-of-divided}.  Since $2 \le m' \le p-3$ and $m'$ is even, this
is a Bernoulli witness in Kummer's range, and $p$ is irregular by
\cref{thm:irregular-of-bernoulli-witness}.
\end{proof}

n41874.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Put $M = C(S)\cdot 2^t$ with $t$ chosen by
\cref{cor:bernoulli-large-multiple} so that $|B_M/M| > 1$.  By
\cref{lem:num-prime-of-large} some prime $p$ divides
$\operatorname{num}(B_M/M)$.  By \cref{thm:vonstaudt-not-dvd-divided},
$(p-1)\nmid M$; in particular $p \ne 2$.  If $p$ were in $S$, then
$(p-1)\mid C(S)\mid M$ by \cref{lem:irregular-base-mem}, a contradiction; so
$p \notin S$.  The divisibility $(q-1)\mid M$ for $q \in S$ is again
\cref{lem:irregular-base-mem}.
\end{proof}

n41876.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
Take the prime $p$ and the index $M$ of \cref{thm:carlitz-numerator-prime}.
Then $p$ is irregular by \cref{thm:carlitz-criterion} and $p \notin S$.
\end{proof}

n41878.content:

By \cref{thm:carlitz-escape} no finite set contains all irregular primes, so
the set is infinite by \cref{lem:infinite-of-escape}.
\end{proof}
